stories.title: Spark Wholesale launches Auckland data centre link
stories.summary: Private fibre links across Auckland will let data-heavy businesses move traffic between facilities with less congestion and more predictable performance.
stories.content:
# Spark Wholesale launches Auckland data centre link

Thu, 10th Sep 2026 (Today)

Spark Wholesale has launched a data centre interconnect service across Auckland using Ciena technology, aimed at organisations moving large volumes of data between data centres.

The service provides private, uncontended connectivity between regional facilities across Auckland. Its initial footprint runs from Silverdale in the north to Papakura in the south, with services available at 10G, 100G, and 400G.

The launch comes as investment in New Zealand data centre infrastructure rises. Industry figures cited by the companies show 56 data centres are operating in the country, with another 20 in development and an expected NZD $10 billion to be invested in data centre growth over the next decade.

Spark Wholesale is using Ciena's WaveLogic 6 Extreme coherent optics on the Waveserver platform for the service. The system is designed for data centre interconnect deployments across metro, regional, and longer-distance networks.

Ciena's technology supports transmission rates of up to 1.6Tb/s, while the Auckland service will support speeds from 10G to 800G. The 800G option is expected to be introduced after the initial launch.

The service is intended for organisations linking critical infrastructure across multiple sites, including cloud and data-intensive workloads. Private connectivity between data centres is becoming more important for operators and enterprise customers as growing use of artificial intelligence tools and cloud services increases demand for bandwidth and more predictable network performance.

### Growing demand

Auckland has become a focal point for data centre expansion in New Zealand, reflecting wider demand from domestic businesses, international carriers, and large cloud providers. That growth has increased the need for links between facilities that can handle larger data volumes while giving customers more control over traffic than shared public network routes.

The new service is part of Spark Wholesale's response to that demand. Alongside the optical transport equipment, it is also using Ciena's Navigator Network Control Suite to manage the network.

The software gives Spark Wholesale visibility and management tools across the service, including support for automated capacity planning, service fulfilment, and fault troubleshooting.

Raj Singh, Tribe Lead, Spark Wholesale, described the project as part of a broader infrastructure investment effort.

“New Zealand's digital future is full of opportunity. Together, Ciena and Spark Wholesale are creating the high-performance foundations that will help organisations harness AI, accelerate innovation and confidently scale for what's next. We're excited to be investing in the infrastructure that will power the next generation of growth across New Zealand,” said Raj Singh, Tribe Lead, Spark Wholesale.

The agreement also underlines Ciena's push in the Australia and New Zealand market, where telecoms operators and wholesale providers are upgrading fibre networks to serve data centres and cloud traffic.

Matt Vesperman, Vice President, Australia, New Zealand, and the Pacific Islands, Ciena, highlighted the country's role in the regional market.

“New Zealand is emerging as a strategic regional hub for hyperscale and AI data centres,” said Matt Vesperman, Vice President, Australia, New Zealand, and the Pacific Islands, Ciena. “Spark is taking advantage of this opportunity, creating a foundation for delivering high-speed DCI services with Ciena's WaveLogic technology.”

For Spark Wholesale, the new interconnect product adds to its portfolio for international carriers, New Zealand telecommunications providers, and channel partners, which use its fixed and wireless network services to support digital services for their own end users.

The launch of a dedicated Auckland interconnect service reflects how network operators are adapting to a market where data centre traffic is becoming more concentrated and more demanding. With more facilities under development and larger data loads moving between them, transport links within metro areas are becoming as important as long-haul international and domestic backbone routes.

Initial availability from Silverdale to Papakura gives Spark Wholesale coverage across the main Auckland corridor, where many of the city's existing and planned data centre sites are located.

stories.title: Energy reform central to Malaysia's economic policy, says minister
stories.summary: Energy reform can no longer be viewed solely as a sectoral or regulatory matter, but must be recognised as an integral part of Malaysia’s broader economic agenda, said Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 9): Energy reform can no longer be viewed solely as a sectoral or regulatory matter, but must be recognised as an integral part of Malaysia’s broader economic agenda, said Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir.

“Energy reform is no longer only a sectoral or regulatory matter. It is central to economic policy,” he said at the Energy Regulatory Insights 2026 forum organised by the Energy Commission.

He noted that the cost, reliability and carbon profile of energy would increasingly influence investment decisions, industrial competitiveness, technology deployment and the ability to protect the interests of the people.

Akmal Nasrullah outlined three key priorities for the next phase of reform: building a competitive and progressive energy market, modernising the electricity grid, and treating energy efficiency as an energy resource in its own right.

Developing a competitive and progressive energy market, the minister noted, requires a clear, predictable regulatory framework with transparent access arrangements.

Such regulations are necessary to shield consumers and maintain system reliability while offering the legal certainty that private entities need to invest capital and innovate, he said.

Akmal Nasrullah said expanding generation capacity requires a modernised, intelligent, and visible power grid. Upgrading this infrastructure, he said, is vital to stabilise variable renewable energy, manage battery storage systems, and safely integrate high-demand industrial consumers like artificial intelligence (AI) data centres.

At the same time, scaling up power generation demands a modern, intelligent, and secure electricity grid. This infrastructure overhaul is essential to balance fluctuating renewable energy, manage battery storage, and safely accommodate high-demand users.

The minister added that the government elevates energy efficiency into a primary resource. By actively curbing power waste, the nation aims to reduce corporate operational expenses, relieve grid strain, and cut greenhouse gas emissions, he said.

“Efficiency reduces operating costs, eases pressure on the system and strengthens competitiveness,” Akmal Nasrullah noted.

The two-day Energy Regulatory Insights forum brought together policymakers, regulators, industry players, investors, and others to discuss the reforms needed to strengthen Malaysia’s energy system and support long-term economic growth.

Edited ByS Kanagaraju

stories.title: Nvidia-backed firm in Indonesia signs US$3.1b GPU loan
stories.summary: Zankore, an Indonesian AI infrastructure platform backed by Nvidia, has signed a US$3.1 billion loan agreement to fund purchases of advanced chips. The transaction is one of the largest chip-financing deals in Asia and reflects rapidly rising demand for computing capacity in the region.
stories.why_it_matters: A debt package of this size signals that lenders are now comfortable underwriting AI hardware risk in Southeast Asia, not just real estate. It lowers the cost of capital for Indonesian GPU clouds and pressures regional rivals to secure similar financing or fall behind on capacity.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Sept 9): Zankore, an Indonesian AI infrastructure platform backed by Nvidia Corp, signed a US$3.1 billion (RM12.6 billion) loan deal on Wednesday to purchase advanced chips, underscoring surging demand for computing capacity across Asia.

Citigroup Inc, ING, Natixis, Qatar National Bank and United Overseas Bank Ltd underwrote the loan, one of Asia’s largest AI infrastructure financing, according to a statement by Zankore. Citigroup is the sole debt adviser on the deal.

Proceeds will be used to acquire and deploy advanced Nvidia graphics processing units in the company’s new AI factory, which will have an initial capacity of 100 megawatts before expanding to one gigawatt.

GPU financing is emerging as the next frontier for AI lenders, as banks and private credit expand beyond data centres to the hardware that powers them. Bank-led deals have been scarce in Asia, where uncertainty over the residual value of chips and geopolitical risks amid US-China technology rivalry remain key obstacles.

Zankore’s financing carries a revenue-sharing and credit-support model from Nvidia, which would ease lenders’ concerns over repayment and credit risk.

“Nvidia is helping us to make it financeable,” Vikram Sinha, chairman of Zankore, said in an interview. Nvidia’s service order will ensure that the computing capacity can be extended to not only investment grade customers but “small enterprises who need compute on demand,” he said.

Nvidia launched the model in July to help its partners broaden access to data center infrastructure and provide financial support for smaller AI players.

Apart from Nvidia, Zankore’s shareholders include Indonesia’s second-largest mobile carrier Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison Tbk, Ooredoo Group and Nokia.

stories.title: S&P sees Malaysian data centre operators tapping offshore US dollar bonds as local banks tighten financing
stories.summary: S&P Global Ratings expects Malaysian data centre operators to begin issuing offshore US dollar bonds in the near future as domestic banks grow more selective about financing increasingly large projects. The ratings agency notes that deal sizes in the sector have outgrown what local bank balance sheets are comfortable absorbing.
stories.why_it_matters: A shift to offshore bond issuance would change who funds Malaysia's data centre build-out and at what cost, exposing operators to currency and rate risk they have so far avoided. Investors and developers should watch the first issuance as a pricing benchmark for the entire sector.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 9): Malaysian data centre operators could turn to the offshore US dollar bond market for funding “quite soon” as local banks become increasingly selective in financing a sector where data centre deals continue to grow in size, according to S&P Global Ratings.

S&P Global Ratings director of financial institutions ratings Nikita Anand said that with data centre exposure accounting for only 1% of total loans currently, Malaysian banks are not yet close to their lending limits.

“Generally, banks are not approaching their sectoral or single counterparty exposure limits yet, but we understand that this could be a constraint, especially for banks which are smaller and have a smaller capital base. It can limit their ability to lend further,” Anand said during S&P Global Ratings’ Spotlight on Emerging Markets webinar on Wednesday.

S&P Global Ratings director of corporate ratings Yijing Ng said the first such deals in Malaysia or the wider Asia-Pacific market are likely to be structured more conservatively as investors become familiar with data centre financing.

“Our expectation is that the first deal that hits Malaysia or the Apac market would likely be a little bit more conservative, a little bit more protected, as investors seek familiarity and comfort at first,” she said.

According to S&P, Malaysia’s data centre industry is expanding rapidly, with capacity projected to exceed 4,500 megawatts (MW) by 2030, driven by strong demand for cloud services and artificial intelligence (AI) workloads, as well as Malaysia’s strategic advantage as a hub close to Singapore.

To achieve this scale, the credit rating agency said the industry could face sizeable funding requirements. This funding is expected to support powered shells, power and cooling infrastructure, and equipment.

S&P had previously estimated that Malaysia’s data centre sector could require more than US$20 billion (RM81.3 billion) in funding over the next three years.

As a result, developers are expected to explore alternative funding sources, including project financing, private credit and offshore US dollar bond markets to bridge the funding gap.

These financing channels will be crucial to sustaining Malaysia’s data centre build-out, ensuring that capacity additions are delivered on time and aligned with the country’s digital agenda.

stories.why_zh: 转向离岸债券发行将改变马来西亚数据中心建设的资金来源及其成本，使运营商面临迄今一直在规避的汇率和利率风险。投资者和开发商应密切关注首次发行，它将成为整个行业的定价基准。

stories.title: OpenAI says working with Samsung on next-generation chips, deepening cooperation
stories.summary: OpenAI is expanding its partnership with Samsung Electronics as it develops proprietary chips, broadening cooperation beyond memory supply into semiconductors and enterprise AI services. The announcement was made in Seoul as the ChatGPT maker deepens ties with South Korean technology firms.
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI's move to design its own silicon with Samsung's help reduces its dependence on Nvidia and reshapes supplier relationships across the AI value chain. For Samsung, the tie-up strengthens its foundry and memory businesses against TSMC and SK Hynix at a critical moment in the AI chip race.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
SEOUL (Sept 9): OpenAI is deepening cooperation with Samsung Electronics as the ChatGPT maker develops its own chips, expanding ties with the South Korean technology giant across semiconductors and enterprise AI services.

"One of the areas where we have made the most progress and gained the most recognition with Samsung Electronics is our joint production and research on the next-generation chips we are developing," Harrison Kim, general manager of OpenAI Korea, said at a press conference in Seoul on Wednesday, without elaborating.

Kim also said Samsung Electronics was "one of the largest-scale deployments of ChatGPT globally," saying the company's employees in Korea and overseas use ChatGPT for work across research and development, marketing and sales.

Samsung Electronics said in a statement that it could not confirm information related to customers.

In June, OpenAI unveiled its first custom artificial intelligence chip designed with Broadcom. OpenAI's engineers designed the chip, called Jalapeno, together with Broadcom for a task known as AI inference, the process of crunching data to answer queries in applications such as ChatGPT.

OpenAI at that time said that Taiwan's TSMC would manufacture the chips.

Last year, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix signed letters of intent to supply memory chips for OpenAI's Stargate data centre project.

Kim said demand for memory chips would continue to grow as more advanced chips were needed to enable faster and more complex computing, making cooperation with South Korean semiconductor suppliers a priority for OpenAI's local office.

The cooperation comes as Samsung broadens its use of generative AI. The company said in June that workers in its Device eXperience division, which oversees mobile phones, televisions and home appliances, would be allowed to use ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Anthropic's Claude internally.

OpenAI said the number of ChatGPT Enterprise users at South Korean companies and institutions had surged about 28-fold as of the end of August from a year earlier, as businesses broadened their use of artificial intelligence from individual tasks to company-wide operations.

Companies were increasingly using AI across functions including legal, sales, finance, marketing and operations, OpenAI said. The company declined to provide absolute user numbers.

South Korea had the largest number of paying ChatGPT subscribers outside the United States as of late last year, according to OpenAI.

OpenAI expects adoption to accelerate following the Sept 4 launch of GPT-6 Astra, its latest model, which it said offered improved performance in computer use, professional work, science, coding and cybersecurity.

stories.title: MN Holdings among big winners as Malaysia builds up power infrastructure — analyst
stories.summary: Hong Leong Investment Bank has identified MN Holdings as a major beneficiary of Malaysia's power infrastructure build-out, citing a larger-than-expected pipeline across Tenaga Nasional, data centres and solar projects. The utility engineering firm has submitted record-high tenders worth RM5 billion.
stories.why_it_matters: The data centre boom is now visibly flowing through to Malaysia's grid contractors, not just developers and landlords. Record tender volumes suggest utility-scale power work will be a multi-year earnings driver, but also raise questions about capacity to deliver and margin pressure as competition bids up.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 9): The pipeline across national electricity utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA), data centres and solar projects is larger than expected, with record-high tenders worth RM5 billion submitted by MN Holdings Bhd (KL:MNHLDG), according to Hong Leong Investment Bank.

The pipeline across Tenaga Nasional, data centres and solar projects is larger than expected, with record-high tenders worth RM5 billion submitted by MN Holdings, according to the research house.

Project call-ups should accelerate in the second half of the year, “although the scale of the pipeline is now larger than we initially anticipated”, the research house said.

Hong Leong Investment lifted its target price for MN Holdings to RM4.65, the highest among four houses covering the stock, while maintaining its 'buy' call.

Shares of MN Holdings, which mainly provides underground utilities and substation engineering services, have been charting new highs this year amid major grid upgrades to cope with a wave of energy-hungry data centres mushrooming in Malaysia.

Malaysia is also accelerating the deployment of large-scale solar projects and increasing the size of each solar farm to drive the transition towards renewable energy.

The stock added another five sen, or 1% to RM3.77 in Wednesday trading. MN Holdings has more than doubled its market capitalisation so far this year to RM2.6 billion.

Tenaga Nasional, its biggest client, has deployed only RM5.6 billion of its RM13 billion regulated capital expenditure target for 2026 and remains committed to deploying the balance over the remaining months, Hong Leong Investment said.

“This implies a sizeable step-up in spending,” the house said, noting that MN Holdings has submitted bids for jobs worth around RM2.5 billion to Tenaga Nasional while another three major projects could be coming into the market this year.

stories.title: VicGrid considers peak pricing for data centres and large loads
stories.summary: VicGrid, the transmission planner for the Australian state of Victoria, is consulting on changes to its transmission pricing methodology that would reward large electricity users for cutting or shifting consumption during peak network demand. The proposal would introduce a new operating consideration for large data centres connecting to the state's grid.
stories.why_it_matters: Peak pricing would turn grid flexibility from a courtesy into a cost line for Victorian data centres, favouring operators that can shift workloads or deploy on-site generation and storage. It also previews how other Australian states may manage surging data centre demand on constrained networks.
stories.content:
VicGrid is considering changes to Australian state Victoria’s transmission pricing framework that would give large electricity users an incentive to reduce or shift flexible consumption during periods of high network demand, potentially creating a new operating consideration for large data centres.

The proposed changes form part of VicGrid’s **consultation on the transmission pricing methodology** for the 2028-33 regulatory period. The organisation says the changes are intended to allocate costs fairly, improve use of the transmission network and provide clearer signals to transmission customers and investors while keeping costs down for consumers.

Under the proposed framework, large energy users would face a peak-and-off-peak pricing structure for the network’s non-locational and common services charges, instead of the current flat rate. VicGrid’s consultation paper proposes a peak window of 4pm to 9pm, seven days a week (AEST), with all other hours off-peak.

The price differential would be phased in, moving from a 1:1 peak-to-off-peak ratio in the first two years of the regulatory period to 3:1 by the final year, essentially meaning peak-period charges would eventually be three times higher than off-peak charges. VicGrid says the signal is not provided under the current pricing framework.

VicGrid reckons the proposed structure would not increase the total transmission revenue recovered from non-locational and common services, but would change how those charges vary according to when electricity is consumed.

The proposal does not, however, quantify what this would mean in dollar terms for a specific facility, or how much flexibility data centres or other large users would be expected to provide. “VicGrid is reviewing Victoria’s transmission pricing methodology to make sure it is responding to our changing energy landscape,” a VicGrid spokesperson told W.Media.

“We’re consulting on proposed changes designed to ensure we allocate costs fairly, use the network efficiently, provide clear signals to transmission customers and investors and keep down costs to consumers,” the spokesperson added.

### Shifting consumption

VicGrid said it had not made assumptions about a specific amount of electricity consumption that large users would be able to shift. However, that leaves the potential impact on data centre operators unclear. The consultation paper does not provide an example of the potential dollar difference in transmission costs for a facility that can shift consumption compared with one that can’t.

It is also unclear from the paper how the peak-pricing signal would interact with the separate demand-based charging arrangement used for large customers with a negotiated Contract Agreed Maximum Demand (CAMD), a group the paper identifies as including data centres, since those customers already pay whichever of a demand-based or energy-based calculation is lower.

The question is particularly relevant as Victoria plans for a growing number of large new electricity loads. Data centres are named in VicGrid’s consultation paper among the large loads driving the review of transmission pricing arrangements, but the organisation says: “VicGrid is not seeking to set out where large new loads should locate or how they should respond.”

Transmission pricing already includes a separate locational component, VicGrid said, reflecting differences in the cost of providing transmission services at different points on the network.

The proposed peak-demand signal would therefore sit alongside, instead of replacing, the existing locational component. In practice, that leaves data centre developers facing two separate transmission considerations: the cost associated with where a facility connects, and potentially the cost associated with when its electricity demand occurs.

### Bespoke loads

Separately, the consultation paper also proposes a mechanism aimed at new large bespoke loads like data centres: a “CAMD collar” that would set a minimum demand charge at 90 percent of a customer’s contracted maximum demand.

VicGrid says this is intended to discourage new customers from overstating their future demand requirements when negotiating connection agreements, after finding that actual usage by large loads can lag contracted capacity by a significant margin. This sort of mismatch can potentially leave other transmission customers subsidising network augmentation built to serve demand that never eventuates.

How much flexibility data centres actually have to respond to a peak-pricing signal remains an open question. Potential sources of flexibility could include shifting workloads, using batteries or managing cooling and other electrical loads, but VicGrid has not specified which technologies or operating strategies it expects large users to employ.

Industry body Data Centres Australia said it had looked at the proposal but was not yet in a position to comment, adding that it expected to have a position in the coming weeks. Meanwhile, no final decisions have been made on the pricing methodology. Feedback from the current consultation will inform the draft methodology VicGrid submits to the Australian Energy Regulator for the 2028–33 regulatory period.

stories.summary_zh: 澳大利亚维多利亚州的输电规划机构VicGrid正在就其输电定价方法的调整征求意见，拟对在网络需求高峰时段削减或转移用电负荷的大型电力用户给予奖励。该提案将为接入该州电网的大型数据中心引入一项新的运营考量。

stories.title: Oracle and HPE expand partnership to scale AI data center networking
stories.summary: Oracle and Hewlett Packard Enterprise have expanded their partnership with a multi-year rollout of networking technology across Oracle's global AI infrastructure. The initiative is designed to relieve bandwidth and latency bottlenecks as Oracle builds out GPU-dense cloud clusters.
stories.why_it_matters: Networking has become the binding constraint in large AI clusters, and this deal shows cloud providers are locking in networking suppliers alongside GPU purchases. It strengthens HPE's position in AI infrastructure and signals to investors that Oracle's cloud expansion is entering a capital-intensive execution phase.
stories.content:
HPE, an enterprise technology firm, is expanding its collaboration with Oracle, supplying its routing and switching platforms to Oracle’s AI data centers worldwide through HPE Juniper Networking to support the growing networking demands of these facilities.

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure’s data center and edge networks are already supported by HPE Juniper Networking, providing a solid foundation as Oracle expands its AI superclusters according to a press release. This expansion places significant demand on bandwidth, latency, congestion management, and fault recovery.

“Oracle is building AI infrastructure at extraordinary scale, and HPE is uniquely positioned to support OCI with one of the industry’s most comprehensive networking portfolios for AI data centers,” said Rami Rahim, HPE Executive Vice President, President, and General Manager of Networking. “Together, we are advancing a high-performance networking architecture that helps Oracle address the traffic management, power, space, and operational requirements of increasingly large AI environments.”

“Building AI infrastructure at Oracle’s scale requires an integrated ecosystem where every layer of the stack works together,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Executive Vice President. “HPE Juniper Networking has been an important part of our cloud architecture and now plays a key role in our AI clusters, regional data centers, and edge networks with the scale, performance, and reliability our customers expect.”

In order to assist Oracle sustain high performance and resilience, the two firms are collaborating on intelligent telemetry that delivers insight and visibility into device and fabric behaviour. By being able to detect queue buildup, packet loss, traffic imbalances and component degradation sooner, Oracle can resolve issues faster.

This is especially important considering the number of data centers Oracle is building out across just the US. Its Stargate campus, being built with OpenAI in Abilene, Texas, has already delivered 42 percent of its planned 1.2 GW capacity. Two other sites in Shackelford, Texas, and Doña Ana County, New Mexico, are expected to be delivered in the first half of 2027, and two more situated in Wisconsin and Michigan will be delivered in the second half of 2027.

Cloud computing providers such as Oracle are increasingly investing in infrastructure that powers AI workloads. In 2025, Oracle reserved US$ 40 billion worth of NVIDIA GPUs for its Abilene site to support OpenAI. This hardware shifts the internal structure of data centers as liquid cooling, robust power delivery, and reliable, low-latency networking become requirements rather than optional extras. According to Mordor Intelligence, AI-first digital transformation is pushing the cloud computing market from a value of US$ 1.04 trillion in 2026 to US$ 2.65 trillion by 2031.
stories.title_zh: Oracle 与 HPE 扩大合作，扩展 AI 数据中心网络规模
stories.summary_zh: Oracle与Hewlett Packard Enterprise扩大了合作，将在Oracle全球AI基础设施中部署为期多年的网络技术。该举措旨在随着Oracle建设GPU密集型云集群，缓解带宽和时延瓶颈。
stories.why_zh: 网络已成为大型 AI 集群的制约瓶颈，这笔交易表明云服务商在购买 GPU 的同时也在锁定网络设备供应商。这巩固了 HPE 在 AI 基础设施领域的地位，并向投资者释放信号：Oracle 的云扩张正进入资本密集的执行阶段。

stories.title: Qualcomm and Amazon team up on AI data centre chips
stories.summary: Qualcomm has partnered with Amazon Web Services to develop custom chips for AI data centres, extending the mobile chipmaker's push into server hardware. The collaboration targets lower costs, reduced power consumption and lower latency for AI workloads running on AWS infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal gives Qualcomm a marquee customer for its data centre ambitions and gives AWS another lever to reduce reliance on Nvidia GPUs. If successful, custom silicon alliances like this could compress margins for incumbent chip suppliers and shift bargaining power toward hyperscalers.
stories.content:
.webp>)

Qualcomm has announced a multi-generational collaboration with Amazon focused on customised silicon for AWS AI data centre infrastructure.

The agreement also covers optical connectivity and expanded use of AWS tools by Qualcomm for chip design workloads.

The companies will work together across multiple generations of silicon for large-scale AI data centres, with a particular focus on AI inference. The deal places Qualcomm more directly alongside major cloud providers that are increasingly designing or commissioning custom chips to meet the growing demands of artificial intelligence services.

They are also developing optical connectivity products extending to 1.6T, as well as later-generation designs. Qualcomm said the effort will draw on its serializer-deserializer, or SerDes, technology and optical digital signal processing.

Demand for AI infrastructure has pushed cloud operators to seek gains not only in processors but also in the links connecting servers and networking equipment inside data centres. Faster optical interconnects are becoming more important as AI systems scale up and require more bandwidth between compute, storage and memory resources.

For Amazon Web Services, the collaboration adds to a broader strategy of building and sourcing specialised silicon for AI workloads. Custom chips have become a key area of competition among cloud providers as they seek to manage the cost, performance and energy use of increasingly complex AI models.

Qualcomm, long known for mobile and communications chips, has in recent years expanded into automotive, personal computing and infrastructure markets. The Amazon tie-up signals a deeper push into data centre hardware, where AI investment has driven intense activity among semiconductor suppliers and hyperscale operators.

### Design work

As part of the broader arrangement, Qualcomm plans to expand its use of AWS AI infrastructure for electronic design automation workloads. That includes Amazon Bedrock, which it will use as it seeks to shorten chip design cycles.

Electronic design automation tools are central to semiconductor development, covering tasks such as circuit design, verification and testing. Any reduction in design time can have commercial value in a market where new chip generations are released under heavy competitive pressure.

The announcement also highlights how semiconductor groups are using cloud-based AI services not only as suppliers to cloud platforms, but also as customers. The relationship is becoming more intertwined as chip designers seek larger pools of compute for simulation and design tasks.

Cristiano Amon outlined Qualcomm's view of the infrastructure challenge created by AI growth.

"As AI demand accelerates, data center infrastructure will require advances in both computing and connectivity to deliver greater performance with more efficiency," said Cristiano Amon, President and Chief Executive Officer, Qualcomm. "Qualcomm is pleased to work with AWS on customized silicon and connectivity solutions, bringing decades of leadership in advanced processing and power-efficient compute, to deliver breakthrough performance and enable the next generation of AI infrastructure."

Amazon said the agreement builds on an existing relationship between the two companies.

"This collaboration with Qualcomm Technologies builds on a strong foundation of partnership and reflects our shared commitment to pushing the boundaries of what's possible," said Prasad Kalyanaraman, Vice President, AWS. "By working together on customized silicon and advanced connectivity, we're delivering more performant, efficient, and cost-effective infrastructure for our customers."

The deal comes as the semiconductor and cloud sectors race to secure positions in AI infrastructure, a market spanning processors, networking, optical components and the software systems used to develop them. By combining custom silicon work, optical interconnect development and Qualcomm's use of AWS design resources, the collaboration spans both the supply side and the internal engineering processes behind future chips.
stories.title_zh: Qualcomm 与 Amazon 联手开发 AI 数据中心芯片
stories.summary_zh: Qualcomm已与Amazon Web Services合作开发用于AI数据中心的定制芯片，将这家移动芯片制造商向服务器硬件领域的拓展进一步延伸。该合作旨在降低在AWS基础设施上运行的AI工作负载的成本、功耗和时延。
stories.why_zh: 这笔交易为 Qualcomm 的数据中心雄心赢得了一位标志性客户，也为 AWS 提供了另一个降低对 Nvidia GPU 依赖的杠杆。如果成功，此类定制芯片联盟可能压缩现有芯片供应商的利润率，并将议价能力转向 hyperscaler。

stories.title: OpenAI signs Malaysia data centre deal with Nvidia-backed Firmus
stories.summary: OpenAI has signed a multi-year agreement to lease dedicated AI compute from two Firmus AI Factory sites in Malaysia, pushing the Nvidia-backed developer past 900MW of contracted capacity. The deal will also bring Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin platform to Southeast Asia for the first time.
stories.why_it_matters: The contract validates Malaysia as a frontline market for hyperscale AI deployments and gives local power, land and connectivity providers a clearer demand signal. For OpenAI it secures scarce GPU capacity outside the US, while regional competitors now face a higher bar to win anchor tenants.
stories.content:
- **OpenAI has contracted dedicated AI compute from two Firmus sites in a multi-year Malaysia data centre deal.**
- **The agreement pushes Firmus past 900MW of contracted capacity and brings Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform to Southeast Asia.**

OpenAI has contracted dedicated AI compute capacity from two Firmus AI Factory sites in Malaysia, in a multi-year partnership the Australian infrastructure company announced from Sydney on September 8. The deal makes OpenAI an anchor customer of Firmus and lifts the company’s total contracted capacity across all customers above 900MW, according to the announcement.

Firmus did not disclose the locations of the two Malaysian sites, the megawatts allocated to OpenAI, or the value of the contract. Asked by *Tech Wire Asia* about the site locations, the Malaysian share of contracted capacity, grid supply arrangements and export licensing for the Nvidia systems, the company said it had no further comment beyond the announcement.

The announcement, however, did indicate its broader portfolio now spans seven AI factories across Australia, Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia. Two are operational, in Australia and Singapore, and five are under development with a stated target of ready-for-service within 24 months. Firmus was valued above US$10.5 billion in its last fundraising, backed by Nvidia, Jane Street, Blackstone funds and Coatue Management, and is widely reported to be preparing an Australian listing.

### What the Malaysia data centre sites will run

Firmus said it will deploy Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform at scale across Asia-Pacific as part of the partnership. The facilities will pair Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems with the company’s own HyperCube platform, which combines liquid cooling, mechanical systems and electrification into a repeatable unit. Firmus said the HyperCube is manufactured and prefabricated in regional New South Wales.

The design work, the manufacturing and the prefabrication sit in Australia. What Malaysia contributes to the arrangement is land, grid connection and water, which is the same division of labour that has characterised most of the country’s data centre boom since 2023. Malaysia has become the region’s fastest-growing data centre market, and the buildout has drawn steady scrutiny over electricity and water consumption, particularly in Johor.

Firmus also said it intends to establish an Australian AI Access Program to give eligible researchers and organisations access to compute for work in science, education, agriculture, energy and climate resilience. No equivalent programme was announced for Malaysia, despite the Malaysian sites being the capacity the OpenAI contract is built on.

### Framing versus footprint

Firmus co-founder and co-CEO Tim Rosenfield said the partnership marks “the moment Asia-Pacific becomes a producer of intelligence” rather than a consumer of it, adding that the company had spent seven years building a footprint running from Southeast Asia to Australia.

Sachin Katti, OpenAI’s VP of compute strategy, said the Malaysian facilities would “help us serve growing demand for OpenAI’s products across the region” and globally. On the announced terms, a US frontier lab is renting capacity from an Australian operator running Australian-built hardware systems on Malaysian soil.

Whether that constitutes producing intelligence or hosting someone else depends on questions the announcement leaves open, including how much of the capacity will be available to Malaysian enterprises and researchers once OpenAI’s allocation is met.

stories.title_zh: OpenAI 与 Nvidia 支持的 Firmus 签署马来西亚数据中心协议
stories.summary_zh: OpenAI已签署一项多年期协议，从马来西亚的两个Firmus AI Factory站点租赁专用AI算力，使这家获Nvidia支持的开发商的签约容量突破900MW。该交易还将首次把Nvidia的下一代Vera Rubin平台引入东南亚。
stories.why_zh: 该合同验证了马来西亚作为 hyperscale AI 部署一线市场的地位，并为当地电力、土地和连接服务提供商提供了更明确的需求信号。对 OpenAI 而言，它在美国以外锁定了稀缺的 GPU 容量，而区域内竞争对手如今面临更高的门槛来争夺锚定租户。
